reason: There are 18 high-confidence claims regarding Teghaza 001 supported by multiple independent sources.
story: In 2022, nomadic hunters in the Sahara discovered a rosy stone that scientists now call the Rosetta Stone of Mars. Known as Teghaza 001, this 800-gram meteorite is one of the oldest pieces of the Red Planet ever found, dating back 4.1 billion years. Unlike most Martian meteorites which are relatively young, Teghaza 001 contains ancient zircon crystals from the planet's very first crust. Research led by NASA's Yang Liu revealed that this igneous rock formed from cooling magma and was later altered by liquid water, proving that early Mars had a dynamic water cycle. By matching its chemical signature to data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, researchers identified its origin as the rugged southern highlands. This rare specimen existed when life was first emerging on Earth, providing a unique window into a time when our neighbor may have been habitable.
angle: A rosy rock found in the Sahara is a 4.1-billion-year-old 'Rosetta Stone' containing crystals from Mars's very first crust.

claims.claim: Teghaza 001 was found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022.
The meteorite is approximately 4.1 billion years old.
Teghaza 001 has a distinctive rosy or rose-colored appearance.
The specimen weighs approximately 800 grams or nearly 2 pounds.
It contains zircon crystals that were used for precise age-dating.
The rock is an igneous specimen that formed from cooling magma.
Chemical analysis shows the rock was altered by liquid water in Mars's ancient crust.
Its mineral composition matches data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter for the southern highlands.
The meteorite is considered one of the three most ancient Martian samples found on Earth.
Oxygen isotopes were used to confirm the stone's Martian origin.
The meteorite was nicknamed a 'Rosetta Stone' for Mars by researchers.
Yang Liu from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory served as the lead author for the study.
The rock's age was verified using rubidium and strontium isotopes.
Nomadic meteorite hunters discovered the stone.
Teghaza 001 existed at the same time that life was beginning on Earth.
The meteorite was ejected from Mars by a high-energy impact event.
There are between 400 and 435 known Martian meteorites on Earth.
Teghaza 001 is similar in age to the famous Allan Hills 84001 meteorite.

disputed: The exact crater of origin is debated; while some link shergottites to Mojave or Tooting craters, others identify 13 potential sites in the southern highlands for Teghaza 001 specifically.
The age of shergottites is controversial, with some scientists arguing they are older than radiometric dating suggests, though most accept the younger ages.
